stem: A 67-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is brought in confused and sweaty at 4 pm. She skipped lunch. Her glucose is 38 mg/dL, insulin and C-peptide are both high, and eGFR is 35 mL/min. She takes metformin, pioglitazone, acarbose, sitagliptin and glyburide.
oneliner: 67F + type 2 diabetes + confused, sweaty after skipping lunch + glucose 38 + high insulin and C-peptide + eGFR 35 + on metformin, pioglitazone, acarbose, sitagliptin, glyburide → which drug?
ask: Which of her drugs most likely caused this episode?

whyNot.A: **Lowers glucose production** without raising insulin; alone it rarely causes hypoglycemia
whyNot.B: **Insulin sensitizer** that needs insulin; low hypoglycemia risk, and insulin here is already high
whyNot.C: **Slows carbohydrate absorption**; does not raise insulin

why: **Hypoglycemia with high insulin and high C-peptide** means the body made insulin. **Glyburide closes beta-cell K-ATP channels** and forces insulin release even without food, and **kidney disease lets its active metabolites accumulate**.

drug.name: Glyburide
drug.how: Closes ATP-sensitive K+ channels on beta cells, so insulin is released regardless of glucose
drug.watch: Hypoglycemia (worse in renal impairment and older adults), weight gain, disulfiram-like reaction

stem: A 44-year-old woman had a total thyroidectomy 6 months ago for a multinodular goiter with compressive symptoms and takes levothyroxine 200 mcg daily. She now has palpitations, tremor, heat intolerance and a 5-kg weight loss. Pulse is 112/min. TSH is 0.1 mU/L and free T4 is high.
oneliner: 44F + thyroidectomy for benign goiter 6 mo ago + levothyroxine 200 mcg + palpitations, tremor, heat intolerance, weight loss + HR 112 + TSH 0.1, free T4 high → what is the best management?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.E: Continue the same dose and add a beta-blocker alone

whyNot.A: **Thionamide**: no thyroid tissue is left to block
whyNot.B: No thyroid tissue remains to take it up
whyNot.D: **Shorter acting, more potent**: would worsen the thyrotoxicosis
whyNot.E: Treats the symptoms, but the **cause is the excess dose**

answer: Iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis from excess levothyroxine; lower the dose
why: **No thyroid gland + suppressed TSH + high free T4 + hyperthyroid symptoms** = overreplacement. **Excess levothyroxine** causes thyrotoxicosis, fixed by **lowering the dose**.

drug.name: Levothyroxine
drug.how: Converted to T3, which binds nuclear receptors and raises metabolic rate
drug.use: Hypothyroidism, thyroid cancer suppression after surgery, myxedema coma
drug.watch: Overreplacement: tachycardia, AF, tremor, weight loss, bone loss; angina in older adults

stem: A 78-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension has fatigue, cold intolerance and a TSH of 38 mU/L. He is started on full weight-based levothyroxine. Two weeks later he has chest pressure on climbing stairs that goes away at rest. Pulse is 104/min, the ECG shows sinus tachycardia without ST elevation, and troponin is normal.
oneliner: 78M + diabetes, hypertension + TSH 38 + full-dose levothyroxine started + 2 wk later exertional chest pressure + HR 104 + normal troponin → which effect?
ask: Which adverse effect of the new drug has most likely occurred?

whyNot.A: Thyroid hormone does not cause **airway narrowing**
whyNot.B: No jaundice or **liver** findings in the stem

why: **Exertional chest pressure with sinus tachycardia and a normal troponin after full-dose levothyroxine.** Thyroid hormone raises **heart rate, contractility and oxygen demand**, which unmasks coronary disease; start low in older vasculopaths.

drug.name: Levothyroxine
drug.how: Converted to T3, which binds nuclear receptors and raises metabolic rate and cardiac beta-receptor sensitivity
drug.watch: Tachycardia, AF, angina in older patients with coronary disease; start low and go slow

stem: A 34-year-old woman with Graves disease has been treated for 6 months. She now has fever and a sore throat with painful mouth ulcers. Her white cell count is 1,800/mm3 with an absolute neutrophil count of 200/mm3. Her medications are propylthiouracil, propranolol, an oral contraceptive, occasional acetaminophen and occasional ibuprofen.
oneliner: 34F + Graves disease treated 6 mo + fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers + ANC 200 + on propylthiouracil, propranolol, oral contraceptive, acetaminophen, ibuprofen → which drug?
ask: Which of her medications most likely caused this?

whyNot.A: **Beta-blocker**: bradycardia and bronchospasm; does not suppress marrow
whyNot.B: Raises **clot risk**; does not cause agranulocytosis
whyNot.E: **NSAID**: stomach and kidney effects; marrow suppression is not typical

why: **Fever + ulcerating pharyngitis + profound neutropenia on a thionamide** = agranulocytosis. This is the dangerous idiosyncratic effect of **propylthiouracil** (and methimazole).

drug.name: Propylthiouracil
drug.how: Blocks thyroid peroxidase (organification) and peripheral T4 to T3 conversion
drug.use: Graves disease, thyroid storm, first-trimester pregnancy
drug.watch: Agranulocytosis, severe hepatotoxicity, ANCA vasculitis; methimazole causes aplasia cutis in the fetus
